title: Chapter 86 – Letters Home
html:
[Green Pine Hill – Lin Wenyuan]

Wenyuan reads the Court's notice standing, because he does not trust himself to sit.

It arrives at noon by the Outer Affairs courier, a gaunt rider on a lathered horse, who dismounts at the gate of Green Pine Hill and hands up a long case of black lacquer with the Arbiter's white seal on the lid. The seal is whole. The case is warm from the rider's chest. Wenyuan carries it across the yard to the hall without a word, past the guards, past the children sweeping the steps, past Hu at the forge door with his iron arm folded across his chest, and shuts the door behind him.

Inside, he breaks the seal.

There are three papers. The first is a single leaf in Shen Wuye's fine, even hand.

To Lin Wenyuan, Patriarch of Green Pine Hill. Notice of Decision. On the thirty-second day after the Spring Register, the Elders of the Azure Cloud Sect, sitting in open session, heard the testimony of Outer Sect Disciple Lin Jian, number 0417, concerning the death of a Blood Shadow of the Well stage at the Fortieth Landing. The Elders find that the disciple acted within the Founders' Rule in defense of the Court. They find further that the disciple's cultivation, measured by the Mirror in open session at the Elders' request, stands at the Ninth Layer of Qi Refining, peak. They find no deception in the disciple's conduct, only reserve. The disciple is confirmed in his place and commended. No further inquiry is made.

A copy of the commendation is enclosed. The Arbiter adds, in his own person, that the disciple's father may be proud.

He reads it three times. Then he sits down after all, on the edge of the long table, with the paper in his hand, and looks at the grain of the wood.

The Ninth Layer. Peak.

He knew. He has known since the night of the Orchard, when the boy walked out of the Garden and the whole hill leaned toward him. He had told himself that he knew. But there is a difference between knowing a thing in the dark and seeing it in the Arbiter's hand, with a white seal, in the grain of an open table, and he finds that his fingers are not quite steady.

Twenty-one years old. The Ninth Layer. A commendation from the Elders.

What is he becoming?

It is the question Qinghe asked her son in the Orchard, and the boy did not answer. Wenyuan has not asked it. He is not sure he wants to.

He sets the notice down and takes up the second paper.

* * *

It is shorter, and it is written on cream-colored stock in a looping, rumpled hand with ink blots at the corners.

To the Patriarch of the Lin Clan, from Bai, Elder of the Pill Hall, Azure Cloud Sect, in his own name and not the Sect's. Patriarch: I will be brief. I am an old man, and I dislike letters.

I have your son as an apprentice. I did not seek him. He arrived, as storms do. He is the best I have seen in ninety years and he is hiding it, which is also correct. I have no intention of telling you what I have seen. You would not believe me, and if you did, you would not sleep.

I write because he needs a thing, and I can get it, and the price is a thing you can pay.

The thing is a vial of Azure dew, three drops, from the Sect Treasury, released by Elder's writ. It is restricted. I will sign the writ. I will sign it in my own name, which is not a small act; I have not signed a restricted writ in nineteen years.

The price is as follows. You hold, at Green Pine Hill, a Garden. It is in trust to the Court for ten years. I do not ask for it. I do not ask for a root, a seed, a leaf or a drop of its water. I ask for a binding promise. When the trust ends, and the Garden returns to your clan's keeping, you will allow the Pill Hall one night in it. One Elder, one furnace, one night. I will name the Elder. You will name the night. We will take nothing that cannot be replaced. I will not say what I mean to do with it. You will have to trust me.

This is a great deal to ask. I am aware of it. I would not ask if I had another coin.

Reply by the next rider. I have a boy who needs the dew by the fifteenth.

Bai.

P.S. He is very polite. It is unnerving.

Wenyuan reads it twice, slowly. He lays it down, face up, on the oiled table, and looks at it for a long time.

A night in the Garden. An Elder, a furnace, one night. In ten years.

What does he want with it?

He thinks of the old man he met only once, at the Hall of Open Session, in the third row of the gallery, a stout rumpled figure eating something from a paper twist. He had seemed, even then, like a person with a secret too large to hide behind plums. I will not say what I mean to do with it. You will have to trust me.

He does not trust him. He does not distrust him either. He trusts the boy, and the boy, evidently, trusts the old man; and in the last two months Wenyuan has learned that it is a risk to question what his son has chosen.

He turns the paper over.

* * *

The third is a letter from Jian, written in a plain small hand.

Father. By the time this reaches you, the Elders will have written. I did not want you to read it from them first. I am well. I am hurt only a little. I have done something I am not going to be able to explain, and I am sorry for the worry.

I need the dew. I do not have another road. If you can pay Bai's price, I will owe you for the rest of my life. If you cannot, I will find another way, and I will not be angry.

The Zhao boy, Hui. I know it is hard. I know what Red Ridge took from us. I would not ask if I did not think the child was not his uncle's. Tell Mother I said so.

Tell Lin Yue the nice count is five now. I forgot Hu.

Jian.

He folds it carefully along its creases and sits for a time with the three letters laid out before him on the table in a row.

A night in the Garden. A seven-year-old Zhao. A promise.

It is, he thinks, the first time his son has asked him for anything.

* * *

He takes it to the clan that evening.

He does it publicly, in the long hall, with every adult who can walk seated on the benches and the children crammed in the doorway. It is a thing his grandfather would have done in a back room. His father would have done it by decree. Wenyuan has learned from the last year, and the last year was a lesson in what happens when a Patriarch keeps a Garden to himself.

He stands on the dais with the three letters in his hand and reads them aloud.

He does not skip the part about the ninth layer. A murmur runs through the hall at the words, a low, wondering, frightened sound, like wind in a barn. He waits for it to pass. He reads Bai's letter. He reads the price. He reads Jian's last line.

"I will not decide this alone," he says, when he has finished.

A pause. Nobody moves.

"The Garden is the clan's," he says. "It has been for a hundred years. My grandfather held it. My father held it. I held it, until the day we lost it, and I held it badly." He keeps his voice level. "I will not be the last man to hold it badly. I do not want to be the man whose successors can say it was Wenyuan's to give. I want it to be yours."

He sets the letters on the table.

"Here is what I propose. The Garden will be entrusted to the clan. Not to me, not to any Patriarch, not to any single hand. A council of seven. Myself. Hu. Wenqing. Wenshi. Qinghe. Two members elected by this hall, one from the village, one from the guard. Any decision that touches the Garden, to give, to sell, to barter, to promise, will be taken by the council, in writing, with the seals of five." He looks around. "It will be done tonight. And the first thing we will decide is Bai's price."

The silence is enormous.

Then, in the third row, an old woman rises. She is Aunt Mei, the oldest woman of the clan, a tiny bent figure in black wool with hands like roots. She has outlived two husbands and five sons. She has never spoken in the hall.

"Patriarch," she says. Her voice is thin and cracked and perfectly clear. "I have a question."

"Aunt."

"Is the boy the one who killed the Blood Shadow?"

A sound goes through the hall like a gasp.

"He is the one who was on the stair," says Wenyuan, carefully. "The Elders say the creature died there."

"Is he the one who walked out of the Orchard in the snow?"

"Yes."

"Then I will vote," says Aunt Mei, "for whatever he wants." She sits down. "And so will everyone in this room who has a head." She folds her hands in her lap. "I am too old to be stupid."

There is a laugh. It is shaky and brief and relieved. It runs along the benches, and the tension breaks.

It takes four hours, in the end. The council is formed. The vote on Bai's price is five to two. Hu is one of the two; he says the old man can have a night in the Garden over his dead body, and then, when it is passed, sits back and says gruffly, "Fine. But I'll be in the room."

When the seals are pressed, Wenyuan goes out into the cold yard and stands alone for some time with his hands behind his back. Snow is falling on the thatch. In the kitchen, a pot is boiling. The sounds of the clan, ordinary, human, tired, come to him through the dark.

It was the right thing.

He does not know if it was the wise thing. But for the first time in a long while, he feels it is a thing that does not belong to him alone.

* * *

Red Ridge sends a delegation on the fourth morning.

They come in a covered cart with six outriders, under a gray flag. Wenyuan receives them in the yard because he will not have them in the hall. There are three. An old man with a cane and a face like a collapsed house, introduced as Zhao Ji, the clan's eldest. A thin gray woman in black. And a steward in a brown tunic, with a bundle of papers and the smooth anxious face of a man who has lived for forty years in the service of other people's secrets.

"Patriarch," says the old man, wheezing. "We come in peace."

"I see six outriders."

"For the road." Zhao Ji's eyes are wet and shrewd. "There are bandits. You know how it is. Since the Court took the lands, there is no one to patrol." He leans on the cane. "We have come to speak of the child."

"Which child?"

"The boy Hui. Seven years of age. A Zhao of the main line. He has been left in the care of our steward, Chu, since his brother went to the Court, and the clan has decided..." The old man pauses to wheeze. "The clan has decided that he should be brought home. To the family. To be raised as a Zhao."

Home.

"He is a ward of the Court," says Wenyuan.

"Since when?"

"Since three days ago." He takes a folded paper from his sleeve and hands it across. It is the Arbiter's order, which arrived by the same rider as the Elders' notice, and which he had not expected: a single line in the fine even hand. The child Zhao Hui, aged seven, is placed under the protection of the Court, and shall be lodged at Green Pine Hill, in the care of the Patriarch, until the Arbiter orders otherwise.

Zhao Ji reads it. He reads it again. His shrewd old eyes sharpen, and for the first time they look afraid.

"The Arbiter," he says.

"Shen Wuye has sent his own deputy," says Wenyuan, "to see it done. He will arrive tomorrow." He keeps his face still. "The Court has been informed that the child's steward is a man of doubtful reliability."

The steward behind the old man has gone pale.

"I am the child's guardian, sir. By the clan's own appointment. I have served the Zhao house for forty..."

"You are called Chu."

"I am."

"You wear a thread at your throat," says Wenyuan, and the man's hand goes to his collar.

It is a guess. He has no way to know. But the steward's face changes in a way that is its own answer, and in the gray woman's, a sudden small flash of fear.

"Zhao Ji," he says, quietly. "I have a letter from your clan's steward-in-chief. Zhao Bei. She was sentenced to the Gray Peak mines for twenty years. She passed through this village two days ago, in a cart, in chains. She asked to speak to me." He holds the old man's eyes. "She told me where the boy was kept. She told me about the thread."

"She had no right..."

"She had every right. She shielded a girl of nine at the culvert, and was struck for it by her own captain. She told me that she would rather spend twenty years in a mine than ten more in a house that did that to children." His voice has not risen. "I am going to ask you to go home. I am going to ask you to tell your clan that the Arbiter's deputy will be at Red Ridge in three days, with six Enforcement guards, to collect the child and the steward. If the child is not there, the Court will take the clan's remaining lands."

The old man stands very still. The steward is trembling.

"You will go quietly, Patriarch Zhao?" says Wenyuan. "Or I can have Lin Hu see you out."

Behind him, at the forge door, there is the slow, deliberate clang of an iron hand on an anvil.

Zhao Ji goes.

* * *

The child arrives on the seventh day, in the arms of an Enforcement guard.

He is very small, very thin, and silent. He wears a gray wool tunic too large for him, and his hair has been cropped close to the skull, and there are shadows under his eyes. He is seven. He looks four. He clings to the guard's neck with both hands and does not look at the yard, or the hall, or the faces that crowd the doorway, and when the guard puts him down, he stands with his arms at his sides and his chin lowered, as if awaiting a blow.

Qinghe goes to him.

She has not said a word since the morning. She kneels on the frozen ground in front of the boy, her skirts spreading in the dirt, and holds out her hands, palms up. She does not touch him. She waits.

"Hui," she says softly. "Your brother says hello."

The child's head lifts.

"He is at the Sect. He is well. He is waiting for you." She smiles. It is her old smile, the one from before the siege, tired and gentle and a little crooked. "He said you were to eat three bowls of millet a day and not argue about it."

A long pause. Then a very small hoarse voice says, "Three?"

"Three."

"I do not like millet."

"No one does." Qinghe's smile widens. "We shall find something else."

The boy looks at her hands for a long moment. Then he steps forward, and lets her take him, and puts his face in her neck. Behind her, the people in the doorway have fallen utterly silent. Somebody is crying. It is Aunt Mei.

Wenyuan stands at the door of the hall with the Arbiter's order in his hand, and does not trust his voice.

Cheng Yun is the one who rode with the guard.

Wenyuan finds him in the yard afterward, at the well, drinking from a gourd with the dust of three days on his cloak. The thin tired face has a little more color than it had in the Hall of Open Session. The badge is back on his collar, a plain iron one, one grade lower than before.

"Restored," he says, in answer to the look. "To the rank below. With a reprimand in the Hall's book that will outlive me." He lowers the gourd. "Elder Duan said that a man who writes one false line in nineteen years and tells the truth about it when asked is a man the Hall can use. He said it with great reluctance."

"I am glad."

"So am I. I did not think I would be." The faint dry smile. "I was in the Hall of Open Session when your son gave his account. Seven Elders. One boy. He said very little." He pauses. "He said that he had asked the stair a question and it answered. Shen wrote it down. Duan did not speak for a minute. Then he asked whether the boy would be willing to say the same thing under the Mirror."

"And?"

"He put his hand on it. It read ninth layer, peak, and nothing else. The Elders looked at one another for a long time." Cheng Yun hangs the gourd on its hook. "They are afraid of him, Patriarch. They are also, I think, very glad. It is an odd combination. I have not often seen it in that room."

Wenyuan looks at the gray sky.

"He is ten," he says.

"Yes." Cheng Yun takes up his reins. "That is what frightens them most."

* * *

Qinghe tells him that night, in the kitchen, with the door shut.

She is sitting at the long table with her hands round a cup of tea gone cold. The pot on the hearth is bubbling. The child is asleep in the back room, in a bed too big for him, with Lin Yue curled at the foot. The fire throws a long gold shadow across her face. She looks, he thinks, like a woman carved from a block of old, patient, gentle wood.

"I am going to the Sect," she says.

He does not say anything.

"I have been deciding for a week. I thought I would decide against it. I thought: he has a father, an uncle, a brother. He has Hu. He has the Pill Hall and an old man with a plum. He does not need me." She turns the cup. "I was wrong. He does need me. Not for protection. He has outgrown that. For the other thing."

"What other thing?"

"To be asked." Her gray eyes lift. "Nobody asks him what he is afraid of. The Elders ask what he has done. You ask whether he is hurt. Feng asks if he is hiding. I ask nothing, Wenyuan. That is the point. I have always asked nothing, and he has always known that he could tell me." She breathes out. "He cannot tell anyone now. He is alone with it. I would like to be in the room."

"The Sect does not admit a Patriarch's wife."

"It admits a medicine supplier with a Court pass." Her mouth curves. "Wenshi holds the trade license for the valley. He says he can write me a letter of appointment as herb-factor for the Pill Hall. Bai has said he will sign the receipts. It is a thin cover, but it is a cover." She sets down the cup. "I will be outside the walls, in the Medicine Valley market. Nobody will notice a woman who sells roots."

"And Lin Yue?"

"Stays with you. With Hui. With Hu." A small, pained smile. "She wanted to come. I said no. She said, then I will give him my knife. It is a very little knife."

He looks at her. The lamp flickers.

"Qinghe."

"Yes."

"If you go," he says slowly, "I will not be able to follow."

"I know."

"The Garden will need me. The council. The clan." He swallows. "I have spent a year learning to share the work. I cannot leave it now."

"I know." She reaches across the table and lays her hand on his. It is dry and warm and steady. "You are not the one who is going to follow. You are the one who stays. It is the hardest part. I would not trade it." She squeezes his fingers. "Hold the hill, Wenyuan. I will hold the boy."

He turns his hand over and closes it on hers.

Outside, the wind has risen, and the snow beats softly on the shutters.

* * *

She leaves at dawn.

It is a gray, bitter morning. The cart waits at the gate, a small covered one drawn by a single mule, with a driver in a straw hat and a trunk of dried herbs in the bed. Two of the Garden's Wardens ride behind, in plain brown, with their swords wrapped in cloth. Hu has packed the trunk himself, and stands beside it with his iron arm hooked in a strap, scowling at the sky.

"Three nights," he says gruffly. "To Willow Bend. Then the Court road. If the snow holds, five days."

"Thank you, Hu."

"I'll send a rider every second day." He clears his throat. "Tell the boy... tell him the thing is nearly done. The spring one. He'll know." He turns his head and spits. "And tell him if he gets hurt again I'll build him a leg."

Qinghe laughs. It is the first real laugh Wenyuan has heard from her in months. She kisses Hu on the cheek, quickly, like a child, and the old man's scarred face goes dark with embarrassment.

She turns to Wenyuan.

He has nothing to say. He has said it all in the night. He puts his hands on her shoulders and looks at her for a long moment, at the clear gray eyes, the small tired lines, the gray streak in her hair he does not remember seeing last week. He kisses her forehead.

"Write," he says.

"Every day."

"Do not lie."

"I never do." She smiles. "I merely select."

She climbs into the cart. The driver clicks his tongue, and the mule leans into the harness, and the wheels creak over the frozen ruts. At the gate, she turns. Her hand lifts, once, a small neat gesture, and then the canvas cover drops.

The cart goes down the lane between the bare pines. The Wardens fall in behind it. The sound of the wheels dwindles.

Wenyuan stands at the gate until it is gone.

When he turns back toward the hall, he finds Lin Yue at his elbow, small and solemn in her quilted short robe, with her hands clasped behind her back. She is looking down the empty road.

"Papa," she says.

"Yes?"

"Mama will be all right. Won't she?"

He opens his mouth to say yes. He closes it.

"I don't know," he says. It is the truth, and she is eight and a half, and she deserves it. "But I think she will make him all right."

Lin Yue nods slowly. After a moment, she slips her hand into his.

The wind lifts the snow from the lane and carries it toward the mountains.
